edges.effect_quant: The modern literature leans protective but not dramatically so. A network meta-analysis of 13 studies involving 85,321 individuals ranked carotenoids among the more favorable nutrients for slowing late AMD progression, while a 20-study systematic review found combinations containing lutein and zeaxanthin associated with better visual-function markers and possible progression benefit. In AREDS2, lutein plus zeaxanthin did not significantly beat placebo in the primary analysis, but it remained a reasonable carotenoid substitute in the AREDS formulation.
edges.population: older adults with intermediate AMD or at risk for progression to advanced age-related macular degeneration
edges.mechanism: Lutein and zeaxanthin accumulate in the macula, where they filter blue light and support antioxidant defense in retinal tissue. That tissue-specific biology makes a modest progression-slowing signal plausible, especially when oxidative stress is contributing to retinal injury.
edges.summary: This edge is supportive rather than dramatic. Lutein and zeaxanthin supplementation appears capable of modestly helping AMD progression-related outcomes in some settings, but the total signal is not strong enough to present as universally disease-modifying.
edges.caveats: Benefits likely depend on disease stage, baseline diet, formulation, and whether supplements are used inside an AREDS-style regimen. The best evidence supports modest progression-related help rather than wholesale prevention of all AMD outcomes.
